tagline.text: The best-known white-sand island of Mercedes' Siete Pecados

location.label: Location
location.text: Off Mercedes, Camarines Norte (Siete Pecados island group)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,500–6,000 (including boat charter, before splitting among the group, rough estimate)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Naga Airport (WNP) or Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL)

children.text: Apuao Grande Island is the best-known of the seven Siete Pecados islands off Mercedes, Camarines Norte. It is known for white sand, a sandbar to a neighboring island, the remains of a resort that closed in the 1980s, and camping.
Apuao Grande Island is the best known of the seven islands scattered off Mercedes, Camarines Norte, the so-called Siete Pecados (Seven Sins). One travel blog says it lies about
10km
northeast of Daet and about
45 minutes

by boat from Mercedes. The seven islands are given as Apuao Grande, Apuao Pequeña, Caringo, Canton, Canimog, Quinapaguian and Malasugui. The waters off Mercedes are also known as home to Irrawaddy dolphins.

The island's appeal is its white-sand beach and simple atmosphere. Behind the beach stand agoho trees, evergreens that resemble pines, and the island is described as having mangrove forest, a sandbar, and a steep cliff on the Pacific side. At low tide a sandbar links Apuao Grande to the neighboring Apuao Pequeña (also called Apuao Munti). Pequeña is about 24.29 hectares with a shoreline of about 350 m, and is known to have a small hill about 150 feet high and a campsite. One guide mentions a 15–20 minute walk to a bat habitat and viewpoint there.

The island also has an unusual history. In its 1980s heyday, the TS Resort was run by the Australian-linked Swagman hotel chain and is said to have had about 30 non-air-conditioned cottages, a restaurant, a beach bar, a swimming pool, a tennis court, a gym, a sauna, a nine-hole golf course and even a small airstrip. Poor marketing and typhoons closed it, and most of its solar-powered villas are now said to be leased to expatriates. Visitors can walk around the remains of the abandoned resort. Conditions and access can change, so check locally.

There is no regular passenger boat, so you need to charter one, and trips depend on weather and sea conditions. Facilities are minimal, so it is safer to bring food, drinking water and a way to charge your devices. Combining it with Bagasbas Beach in Daet, Calaguas and Caramoan makes for a full northern Bicol itinerary. Boat and facility fees differ between guides and much of the material is old, so ask the Mercedes tourism office just before you go. The town of Mercedes is also worth a look. Catches are traded at the fish market beside the port, and a boat-blessing procession called Karakol is held on June 13 and the fishermen's thanksgiving festival Kadagatan on August 1–7. If your dates overlap, see them before or after the island trip. Festival schedules can change from year to year.

The island's beach is white sand, with agoho trees resembling pines behind it. It suits swimming and beach walks, and is a nice place to rest in the shade and look at the sea. On quiet days you can enjoy the peace. When you hop between several islands, Apuao Grande is the biggest base, so many itineraries stop here for lunch and rest.

At low tide a sandbar emerges, and you can reportedly walk to the neighboring Apuao Pequeña. One traveler noted that when crossing before the water had fully drained the current was somewhat strong. Check the tides in advance and set a time to come back.

blocks.title: Remains of the abandoned TS Resort

children.text: Traces of the resort once run by a hotel chain in the 1980s remain. It once even had a golf course and an airstrip, so it is worth a walk imagining the island's past. The buildings may be worn, so do not push your way inside.
Camping on the island is said to be possible. The camping fee is reported at about ₱100–200 and does not include a tent, so bring or rent one. Take all your trash with you.
One guide lists kayaks at

Apuao Pequeña is said to have a 15–20 minute trail to a bat habitat and viewpoint. It can be steep or slippery, so wear proper shoes.
The Siete Pecados also come with stories of a sunset viewing hill on Canton and an underwater cave visible only at low tide. The usual plan is to ask your boatman to link two or three islands.

items.title: Island day trip
items.subtitle: Leave in the morning, return in the afternoon

children.text: Go from your Daet lodging to Mercedes Port by tricycle or jeepney. It is said to take about 10–15 minutes.
Confirm the boat and island fees at the tourism office and set out. Morning, when the sea is calm, is safer.
Arrive on the island, walk the beach and look around the resort ruins.
Check the low-tide time and cross the sandbar to see Apuao Pequeña.
Eat the packed lunch you brought, then swim and kayak.
Board the boat back before the sea gets rough.
It is safest to assume there are no restaurants on the island. Bring food, water and trash bags.

items.title: One-night camping
items.subtitle: Sunset and stars on the island

children.text: Load camping gear and food at Mercedes Port and head to the island.
Set up your tent, have lunch and play in the water.
Stroll the beach at sunset and prepare dinner.
Enjoy the stars and the sound of waves at night, and turn in early.
On day two, watch the sunrise, pack up and head back.
A camping boat is listed at about ₱4,000, but it varies by season, so confirm when you book.

items.title: Boat from Mercedes to the island

children.text: Guides say there is no regular passenger service, so you need to charter a boat. The tourism office at the Mercedes fish port can connect you with one.
From Mercedes to the island is about
45 minutes
according to one blog. It varies with weather and boat type.
The tourism office phone is written differently depending on the source: (056) 444-1261 or (054) 444-1261. Check the area code before calling.

One travel blog recommends late March to early May. This is the dry season, with many calm sea days and clear skies. Northern Bicol is affected by typhoons, so from June to November some days may have no boats.
December to February brings cool winds, and the northeast monsoon can make the sea rough. Check the tides when crossing the sandbar.

During the day the sea is often calmer in the morning, so leaving early and returning in the early afternoon is a sensible plan. Low-tide times differ each day, so check a tide table before leaving and decide with your boatman when to cross the sandbar. It also helps to remember that around the full moon and new moon, tidal differences are larger, so the sandbar may stay exposed longer or flood sooner.

On the island you can stay by camping or in a beach house. One guide lists beach houses at about

per night, but this varies with occupancy and season. Some places rent out tents. For more comfortable sleeping, stay at a hotel in Daet town (Pineapple Island Resort, Nathaniel Hotel, Dolor Hotel, D House Hotel and others) and make the island a day trip.

Assume there is almost no food on the island and bring food and drinking water. You can buy fresh seafood at the fish market and market near Mercedes Port. Mercedes has binut-ong, a rice cake soaked in coconut milk, and one source says the better soaked ones contain more coconut milk. At the fish port you can also watch the day's catch come in.
Mercedes has homestays with local families; a 2015 guide mentions stays in Cayucyucan and Colasi from about

per night. This is old information, so confirm current rates and whether they operate. After your island day you can have a seafood meal near the port, and some people also enjoy kayak surfing at Baybay Beach in Mercedes from August to December.
Prepare cash in advance. It is safer to withdraw in Daet or Naga.
Keep cameras and phones in waterproof packs or dry bags.
Bring plenty of food, drinking water and a power bank.
Take all your trash with you. Assume there is no disposal on the island.
The sandbar disappears with the tide. Set a return time before crossing.
When booking a boat, decide the number of people, the islands to visit and the return time beforehand.
A small boat rocks when there are waves. Bring motion-sickness medicine.
On peak days and weekends boats fill up early. Inquire a few days ahead.
Island trips depend on weather and sea conditions. If a typhoon or strong wind is forecast, postpone, and wear a life jacket aboard.
There is no regular service, so if you miss your return boat you may spend the night on the island.
The current on the sandbar can be strong. Children should cross with an adult.
The abandoned resort buildings may be worn, so do not go inside or climb on them.
There is no medical facility on the island. Bring basic medicines.
Some beaches have little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and a thin long-sleeved shirt.
Fees and contacts come from old sources and may have changed, so check just before you go.
